title: New York Times and other outlets sue web browser Brave over alleged content scraping
content:
The New York Times sued Brave, the 11-year-old, privacy-focused browser company, on Monday, alleging it scraped the outlet’s copyrighted content and unlawfully distributed it to customers the suit names as Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere.
Separately on Monday, the Daily News, the Chicago Tribune, and the Orlando Sentinel filed a similar lawsuit. Both were brought in federal court in Manhattan.
The New York Times, which has also sued OpenAI and Perplexity over similar claims, likens Brave to a “supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content” for AI companies.
“In this way, Brave acts both like a burglar that misappropriates the content of publishers, and an AI ‘fence’ that sells stolen content to third parties,” the suit reads. It says Brave built an index of more than 30 billion web pages using an unidentified crawler, leaving publishers unable to block it.
The suit also targets a Brave browser feature that bypasses paywalls and the company’s practice of blocking publishers’ ads while selling its own.
Founded in 2015, Brave has raised roughly $250 million to date, according to private-market trackers. The Times seeks an injunction and damages.
Brave did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

report.summary: The New York Times and three other newspaper outlets sued Brave, alleging the privacy browser scraped copyrighted content and resold it to AI companies including Anthropic, Perplexity and xAI.
report.background: The lawsuit lands in the middle of a multi-year legal war over how AI models are trained. The Times sued OpenAI in late 2023 and Perplexity in 2024 over similar scraping claims, and a wave of publisher litigation has followed. Most disputes have focused on AI labs themselves; this case targets an intermediary — a browser and search-index company that sits between publishers and model developers. Brave, founded in 2015 and backed by roughly $250 million in venture funding, markets itself as a privacy-first alternative to Chrome and Google Search, and operates its own independent web index. That index, and the crawler that feeds it, are now the center of the dispute. The case also tests whether ad-blocking and paywall-bypassing features, long framed as consumer privacy protections, can be characterized as commercial misappropriation when the same company licenses data to AI firms.
key_points: The core allegation is that Brave used an unidentified crawler to assemble an index of more than 30 billion web pages, then distributed that content to AI developers named in the suit as Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI and Cohere. The Times calls Brave a "supplier, dealer, and distributor" of stolen content.

The filing uses unusually vivid language, describing Brave as both "a burglar that misappropriates the content of publishers" and an "AI fence" that resells stolen material. That framing is designed to make Brave liable not just for scraping but for enabling downstream AI training.

Beyond scraping, the suit targets two signature Brave features: technology that bypasses publisher paywalls, and the browser's practice of blocking publishers' ads while serving its own advertising. The Times argues this deprives outlets of both subscription and ad revenue.

A second, similar suit was filed the same day in Manhattan federal court by the Daily News, the Chicago Tribune and the Orlando Sentinel. The coordinated filings signal a broader publisher strategy of pursuing intermediaries, not only AI labs.

The Times is seeking an injunction and monetary damages. Brave has not publicly responded, and the outcome could hinge on whether its crawler respected robots.txt signals and how its data-licensing deals with AI companies were structured.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the case expands the legal battlefield from model developers to data middlemen. If courts accept the "AI fence" theory, companies that aggregate, index or license web data could face liability even when they did not train a model themselves — raising costs and encouraging more licensing deals. For developers, the practical effect is a shrinking pool of "free" training data and more scrutiny of crawler provenance; expect stronger demand for licensed corpora and documented data lineage. For regular users, features marketed as privacy protections, like ad-blocking and paywall bypass, may become legally contested or get bundled into paid tiers. The case could also shape how much control publishers retain over content once it enters a browser's index.
report.tools: To follow the data-provenance debate, watch Brave Search API and its independent index documentation, plus Common Crawl for how open crawl data is published. Publishers and site owners can use Cloudflare's bot management and AI crawler controls, robots.txt and the Robots Exclusion Protocol, and Spawning's Do Not Train registry to signal training preferences. For legal tracking, the Times v. OpenAI and Times v. Perplexity dockets offer useful precedent context.
